<b>AN INTRODUCTION TO THE TI990 UNIX ASSEMBLER</b>


This document describes the usage and input syntax of the ancient Unix TI990 assembler <b>as</b>.
The details of the TI990 architecture are not described.
The input syntax of this assembler is generally similar to that of the original Ritchie PDP-11 assembler.
The actual code is a derivative of Richard Miller's assembler for the port of Unix to the Interdata 7/32.
This document is a derivative of the Ritchie file note on the Unix assembler. 

The <b>as</b> assembler is a rather ordinary assembler without macro capabilities.
It produces an output file that contains relocation information and a complete symbol table;
thus the output is acceptable to the Unix link-editor <b>ld</b>, which may be used to combine the outputs
of several assembler runs and to obtain object programs from libraries.
The output format has been designed so that if a program contains no unresolved references to external
symbols, it is executable without further processing.

<br>
<b>1. Usage</b>

The command line syntax for <b>as</b> as follows:
<verbatim>
  as [−u] [-l] [−o outfile] infile [,infile]...
</verbatim>
If the optional "−u" argument is given, all undefined symbols in the current assembly will be made
<i>undefined-external</i>. Also see the .globl directive below.
If the optional "-l" argument is given, a listing file is printed to the standard output.
The output of the assembler is by default placed on the file a.out in the current directory;
the optional "−o" flag causes the output to be placed on the named file.
If there were no unresolved external references, and no errors detected, the output file is marked executable;
otherwise, if it is produced at all, it is made non-executable.
The other arguments name files which are concatenated and assembled. Thus programs may be written in
several pieces and assembled together.

<br>
<br>
<b>2. Lexical conventions</b>

Assembler tokens include identifiers (alternatively, "symbols" or "names"), temporary symbols, constants, and operators.

<u>2.1 Identifiers</u>

An identifier consists of a sequence of alphanumeric characters (including period ".", underscore "_",
and tilde " ̃" as alphanumeric) of which the first may not be numeric. Only the first eight characters are significant.
When a name begins with a tilde, the tilde is discarded and that occurrence of the identifier generates a unique entry
in the symbol table which can match no other occurrence of the identifier. This feature is used by the C compiler to
place names of local variables in the output symbol table without having to worry about making them unique.

<u>2.2 Temporary symbols</u>

A temporary symbol consists of a single digit followed by "f" or "b". Temporary symbols are discussed fully in section 5.1.

<u>2.3 Constants</u>

Constants are 16 bit quantities and can have one of four forms:
  *  a constant starting with the sequence "0x" is a hexadecimal number constant.
  *  a constant starting with the digit "0" is an octal constant. A digit larger than 7 terminates the constant.
  *  a constant starting with one of the other digits (i.e. "1" through "9") is a decimal constant
  *  a constant starting with a single quote (') initiates a character constant.

Numeric constants can have any number of digits, but the value is truncated to the lower 16 bits of the resulting number.
The constant is interpreted as a two’s complement value: -1 and 65535 both denote a constant with 16 "1" bits.

A single-character constant consists of a quote followed by an ASCII character not a new-line, followed by another
single quote. Certain dual-character escape sequences are acceptable in place of the ASCII character to represent
new-line and other non-graphics (see String statements, section 5.5). The constant’s value has the code for the
given character in the least significant byte of the word and is null-padded on the left. It is permissible to have
a second ASCII character following the first, to make up a word sized constant. In that case the constant’s value has
the code for the first given character in the least significant byte and that for the second character in the most
significant byte. Character constants with either zero or more than 2 ASCII characters occuring between the opening
and closing quote constitute a syntax error.

<u>2.4 Operators</u>

There are several single character operators; see section 6.

<u>2.5 Blanks</u>

Blank and tab characters may be interspersed freely between tokens, but may not be used within tokens
(except character constants). A blank or tab is required to separate adjacent identifiers or constants not
otherwise separated.

<u>2.6 Comments</u>

The two character sequence "//" (slash-slash) introduces a comment, which extends through the end of the line on
which it appears. Comments are ignored by the assembler.

<br>
<b>3. Segments</b>

Assembled code and data fall into three segments: the text segment, the data segment, and the bss segment.

  *  The text segment is the one in which the assembler begins, and it is the one into which instructions
are typically placed. The UNIX system will, if desired, enforce the purity of the text segment of programs
by trapping write operations into it. Object programs produced by the assembler must be processed by the
link-editor <b>ld</b> (using its "−n" flag) if the text segment is to be write-protected. A single copy of
the text segment is shared among all processes executing such a program.

  *  The data segment is available for placing data or instructions which will be modified during execution.
Anything which may go in the text segment may also be put into the data segment. In programs with write-protected,
sharable text segments, data segment contains the initialized but variable parts of a program. If the text segment
is not pure, the data segment begins immediately after the text segment; if the text segment is pure, the data
segment begins at the lowest 8K byte boundary after the text segment.

  *  The bss segment may not contain any explicitly initialized code or data. The length of the bss segment
(like that of text or data) is determined by the high-water mark of the location counter within it. The bss segment
is actually an extension of the data segment and begins immediately after it. At the start of execution of a
program, the bss segment is set to 0. Typically the bss segment is set up by statements exemplified by
<verbatim>
lab: . = .+10
</verbatim>
The advantage in using the bss segment for storage that starts off empty is that the initialization information
need not be stored in the output file.

The assembler switches between the three segments through the pseudo statements <b>.text</b>, <b>.data</b> and
<b>.bss</b>, which are discussed in section 7.6, 7.7 and 7.8.

Each segment has its own location counter during assembly and the segments are relocated to their sequential
positions at the very end of the assembly process (and possibly again by the link-loader <b>ld</b>). See also
section 4, Location counter and section 5.4, Assignment statements.

<br>
<b>4. The location counter</b>

One special symbol, ".", refers to the location counter of the current segment. Its value at any time is
the offset within the appropriate segment of the start of the statement in which it appears. The location
counter may be assigned to, with the restriction that the current segment may not change.

<br>
<b>5. Statements</b>

A source program is composed of a sequence of statements. Statements are separated either by newlines or by
semicolons. There are five kinds of statements:
  *  null statements
  *  expression statements
  *  assignment statements
  *  string statements
  *  keyword statements.

Any kind of statement may be preceded by one or more labels.

<u>5.1 Labels</u>

There are two kinds of label: name labels and numeric labels. A name label consists of a name followed by
a colon (":"). The effect of a name label is to assign the current value and type of the location counter (".")
to the name. An error is indicated in the first pass if the name is already defined; an error is indicated in
subsequent passes if the (".") value assigned changes the definition of the label.

A numeric label consists of a digit 0 to 9 followed by a colon (":"). Such a label serves to define temporary
symbols of the form "<i>n</i>b" and "<i>n</i>f", where <i>n</i> is the digit of the label. As in the case of
name labels, a numeric label assigns the current value and type of "." to the temporary symbol. However, several
numeric labels with the same digit may be used within the same assembly. References of the form "<i>n</i>f" refer
to the first numeric label "<i>n</i>:" <u>f</u>orward from the reference;
"<i>n</i>b" symbols refer to the first "<i>n</i>:" label <u>b</u>ackward from the reference. This sort of temporary
label was introduced by Knuth in "The Art of Computer Programming, Vol I: Fundamental Algorithms". Such labels
tend to conserve both the symbol table space of the assembler and the inventive powers of the programmer.

<u>5.2 Null statements</u>

A null statement is an empty statement (which may, however, have labels). A null statement is ignored by the
assembler. Common examples of null statements are empty lines or lines containing only a label.

<u>5.3 Expression statements</u>

An expression statement consists of an arithmetic expression not beginning with a keyword. The assembler computes
its (16-bit) value and places it in the output stream, together with the appropriate relocation bits.

<u>5.4 Assignment statements</u>

An assignment statement consists of an identifier, an equals sign ( = ), and an expression. The value and type of
the expression are assigned to the identifier. It is not required that the type or value be the same in pass 2 as
in pass 1, nor is it an error to redefine any symbol by assignment.

Any external attribute of the expression is lost across an assignment. This means that it is not possible to declare
a global symbol by assigning to it, and that it is impossible to define a symbol to be offset from a non-locally
defined global symbol.

As mentioned, it is permissible to assign to the location counter ".". It is required, however, that the type of
the expression assigned be of the same type as ".", and it is forbidden to decrease the value of ".".
In practice, the most common assignment to "." has the form ". = . + n" for some number n; this has the effect
of generating n null bytes.

<u>5.5 String statements</u>

A string statement generates a sequence of bytes containing ASCII characters. A string statement consists of a double
quote <b>"</b> followed by a sequence of ASCII characters not including newline, followed by a closing double quote
<b>"</b>. Any of the ASCII characters may be replaced by a two-character escape sequence to represent certain
non-graphic characters, as follows:
<table>
<tr><td><u>Escape</u></td><td><u>Hex</u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</td><td><u>Meaning</u></td></tr></b>
<tr><td>\n</td><td>0x0a</td><td>newline</td></tr>
<tr><td>\r</td><td>0x0d</td><td>carriage return</td></tr>
<tr><td>\t</td><td>0x0b</td><td>horizontal tab</td></tr>
<tr><td>\v</td><td>0x0c</td><td>vertical tab</td></tr>
<tr><td>\0</td><td>0x00</td><td>null</td></tr>
</table>

All other characters following a \ represent themself, i.e. \\ denotes a single backslash and \" denotes a double quote.
The latter does not terminate the string, but becomes a character of the string. The same escape sequences may also be
used within singlea nd double-character constants (see section 2.3 above).

<u>5.6 Keyword statements</u>

Keyword statements are numerically the most common type, since machine instructions are of this sort. A keyword
statement begins with one of the many predefined keywords of the assembler; the syntax of the remainder depends on
the keyword. Section 8 discusses machine instructions and their syntax in more detail.

<br>
<b>6. Expressions</b>

An expression is a sequence of symbols representing a value. Its constituents are identifiers, constants,
temporary symbols, operators, and brackets. Each expression has a type.
All operators in expressions are fundamentally binary in nature; if an operand is missing on the left,
a 0 of absolute type is assumed. Arithmetic is two’s complement and has 16 bits of precision. All
operators have equal precedence, and expressions are evaluated strictly left to right; parentheses are
reserved for addressing modes and cannot be used for expression grouping.

<u>6.1 Expression operators</u>

The operators are:
<table>
<tr><td>+</td><td>addition</td></tr>
<tr><td>-</td><td>subtraction</td></tr>
<tr><td>*</td><td>multiplication</td></tr>
<tr><td>/</td><td>division</td></tr>
<tr><td>|</td><td>bitwise or</td></tr>
<tr><td>&</td><td>bitwise and</td></tr>
</table>
All operators work on 16 bit two's complement words and overflow is not detected.

<u>6.2 Types</u>

The assembler deals with a number of types of expressions. Most types are attached to keywords and used
to select the routine which treats that keyword. The types likely to be met explicitly are:
  *  <u>undefined</u>: Upon first encounter, each symbol is undefined. It may become undefined if it is
assigned an undefined expression. It is an error to attempt to assemble an undefined expression in pass 2;
in pass 1, it is not (except that certain keywords require operands which are not undefined).

  *  <u>undefined external</u>: A symbol which is declared <b>.globl</b> but not defined in the current
assembly is an undefined external. If such a symbol is declared, the link editor <b>ld</b> must be used to
load the assembler’s output with another routine that defines the undefined reference.

  *  <u>absolute</u>: An absolute symbol is defined ultimately from a constant. Its value is unaffected
by any possible future applications of the link-editor to the output file.

The value of a text symbol is measured with respect to the beginning of the text segment of the program. 
  *  <u>text</u>: The value of a text symbol is measured with respect to the beginning of the text segment
of the program. If the assembler output is link-edited, its text symbols may change in value since the
program need not be the first in the link editor’s output. Most text symbols are defined by appearing
as labels. At the start of an assembly, the value of "." is text 0.

  *  <u>data</u>: The value of a data symbol is measured with respect to the origin of the data segment of a program.
Like text symbols, the value of a data symbol may change during a subsequent link-editor run since previously
loaded programs may have data segments. After the first .data statement, the value of "." is data 0.

  *  <u>bss</u>: The value of a bss symbol is measured from the beginning of the bss segment of a program.
Like text and data symbols, the value of a bss symbol may change during a subsequent link-editor run,
since previously loaded programs may have bss segments. After the first .bss statement, the value of "." is bss 0.

  *  <u>external absolute, text, data, or bss</u>: Symbols declared .globl but defined within an assembly
as absolute, text, data, or bss symbols may be used exactly as if they were not declared .globl; however,
their value and type are available to the link editor so that the program may be loaded with others that
reference these symbols.

The assembler does not have a separate type for registers: these are refered to by an absolute value in
the range 0 to 15. The assembler predefines the symbols <b>r0</b> through to <b>r15</b> with these values
to make source code easier to read. As a consequence, one can refer to r3 as "r0+3".
<b>sp</b> is a synonym for <b>r15</b> and <b>bp</b> is a synonym for <b>r14</b>.

Each keyword known to the assembler has a type which is used to select the routine which processes the
associated keyword statement. The behavior of such symbols when not used as keywords is the same as if
they were absolute.

<u>6.3 Type propagation in expressions</u>

When operands are combined by expression operators, the result has a type which depends on the types of
the operands and on the operator. The rules involved are complex to state but were intended to be sensible
and predictable. For purposes of expression evaluation the important types are
  *  undefined
  *  absolute
  *  text
  *  data
  *  bss
  *  undefined external
  *  other

The combination rules are then:
  *  If one of the operands is undefined, the result is undefined.
  *  If both operands are absolute, the result is absolute. If an absolute is combined with one of
the "other types" mentioned above, the result has the other type.
  *  If two operands of "other type" are combined, the result has the numerically larger type
  *  An "other type" combined with an explicitly discussed type other than absolute acts like an absolute.

Further rules applying to particular operators are:
  *  "+": If one operand is text-, data-, or bss-segment relocatable, or is an undefined external,
the result has the postulated type and the other operand must be absolute.
  *  "−": If the first operand is a relocatable text-, data-, or bss-segment symbol, the second operand
may be absolute (in which case the result has the type of the first operand); or the second operand may
have the same type as the first (in which case the result is absolute). If the first operand is external
undefined, the second must be absolute. All other combinations are illegal.

<br>
<b>7. Pseudo-operations</b>

The keywords listed below introduce statements that generate data in unusual forms or influence the later
operations of the assembler. The meta notation "<nowiki>[stuff]...</nowiki>"
means that zero or more instances of the given stuff may appear. Also, boldface tokens are literals,
italic words are substitutable.

<b>7.1 .byte</b> <i>expression <nowiki>[ ,expression]...</nowiki></i>

The expressions in the comma-separated list are truncated to 8 bits and assembled in successive bytes. The
expressions must be absolute. This statement and the string statement above are the only ones that
assemble data one byte at at time.

<b>7.2 .even</b>

If the location counter "." is odd, it is advanced by one so the next statement will be assembled at a word
boundary.

<b>7.3 .if</b> <i>expression</i>

The <i>expression</i> must be absolute and defined in pass 1. If its value is nonzero, the <b>.if</b> is
ignored; if zero, the statements between the <b>.if</b> and the matching <b>.endif</b> (below) are ignored.
<b>.if</b> may be nested. The effect of <b>.if</b> cannot extend beyond the end of the input file in which
it appears.

<b>7.4 .endif</b>

This statement marks the end of a conditionally-assembled section of code. See <b>.if</b> above.

<b>7.5 .globl</b> <i><nowiki>name [, name]...</nowiki></i>

This statement makes the names external. If they are otherwise defined (by assignment or appearance as a
label) they act within the assembly exactly as if the <b>.globl</b> statement were not given; however, the link
editor <b>ld</b> may be used to combine this routine with other routines that refer these symbols.

Conversely, if the given symbols are not defined within the current assembly, the link editor can combine
the output of this assembly with that of others which define the symbols. As discussed in section 1, it is
possible to force the assembler to make all otherwise undefined symbols external.

<b>7.6 .text</b>

<b>7.7 .data</b>

<b>7.8 .bss</b>

These three pseudo-operations cause the assembler to begin assembling into the text, data, or bss segment
respectively. The location counter is made even, i.e. after sitching segment, an <b>.even</b> statement is
implied. Assembly starts in the text segment. It is forbidden to assemble any code or data into the
bss segment, but symbols may be defined and "." moved about by assignment.

<b>7.9 .comm</b> <i>name , expression</i>

Defines and external symbol of size <i>expression</i>. In effect, <i>name</i> behaves in the current assembly
just like an undefined external. However, the link-editor <b>ld</b> has been special-cased so that all external
symbols which are not otherwise defined, and which have a non-zero value, are defined to lie in the bss segment,
and enough space is left after the symbol to hold expression bytes. All symbols which become defined in this way
are located before all the explicitly defined bss-segment locations.

<br>
<b>8. Machine instructions</b>

The assembler implements all instructions of the TMS9995 processor and several synthetic instructions. The latter
can be thought of as built-in macro's.

<u>8.1 Instruction mnemonics</u>

All the standard mnemonics of the TMS9995 processor are supported. The mnemonics must be in lowercase in order
to be recognised, i.e. "lwpi" is an instruction mnemonic, "LWPI" is an undefined symbol.

<u>8.2 Operands</u>

The assembler uses a different operand syntax than the standard Texas Instruments syntax for the TI990. The
relationship is shown below:
<table>
<tr><td><b>Mode</b></td><td><b>as syntax</b></td><td><b>TI syntax</b></td><td><b>Example</b></td><tr>
<tr><td>register</td><td>rn</td><td>RN</td><td>mov r0,r1</td><tr>
<tr><td>indirect</td><td>(rn)</td><td>*RN</td><td>dec (r1)</td><tr>
<tr><td>auto increment&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</td><td>(rn)+</td><td>*RN+</td><td>clr (r1)+</td><tr>
<tr><td>direct</td><td>@name</td><td>@NAME</td><td>s r0,@var</td><tr>
<tr><td>indexed</td><td>@name(rn)&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</td><td>@NAME(RN)&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</td><td>mov @table(r1),r0</td><tr>
<tr><td>immediate</td><td>expr</td><td>expr</td><td>lwpi len+1</td><tr>
<tr><td>relative</td><td>expr</td><td>expr</td><td>jmp .+2</td><tr>
</table>

Note that an absolute expression evaluating to a number between 0 and 15 is acceptable whereever a register is
required and that names could be offset by an absolute constant. Relative expressions in jumps must be within
-128 to +127 words from "." in the current segment. Relative expressions in CRU instructions must be absolute
and lie between -128 and +127.

<u>8.3 Extended branch instructions</u>

The assembler accepts a set of synthetic instructions for conditional branches that work both with near (within
-128 to +127 words) and far (all other) destinations:
<table>
<tr><td><b>Mnemonic&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</b></td><td><b>Meaning</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>bjmp</td><td>branch or jump unconditionally</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjeq</td><td>branch or jump on equal</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjne</td><td>branch or jump on not equal</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjlt</td><td>branch or jump on signed less than</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjls</td><td>branch or jump on signed less or same</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjgt</td><td>branch or jump on signed greater</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjgs</td><td>branch or jump on signed greater or same</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjl</td><td>branch or jump on unsigned lower</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjle</td><td>branch or jump on unsigned lower or equal</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjh</td><td>branch or jump on unsigned higher</td></tr>
<tr><td>bjhe</td><td>branch or jump on unsigned higher or equal</td></tr>
</table>

These instructions are either implemented as one or two conditional jump instructions, or as the reverse
conditional jump(s) over an unconditional branch condition. The "bjmp" instruction expands to either "jmp" or
"b" depending on the destination distance.

<u>8.4 Other instructions</u>

The assembler accepts one special instruction mnemonic, "sys". This instruction takes a single, unadorned
argument and currently expands to a "xop 1" instruction:

  *  "sys 23" expands to "xop @23,1"

This instruction is used to trap into the operating system. It has been added a macro to make it easy to
vary the trap mechanism for various implementations of the TI990 architecture. An alternative trap
mechanism could work with external instructions.

<br>
<b>9. Errors</b>

When an input file cannot be read, its name followed by a question mark is typed and assembly ceases.
When syntactic or semantic errors occur, a diagnostic is typed out together with the line number and
the file name in which it occurred. Errors in pass 1 cause cancellation of pass 2.
The possible errors are:

  *  "Previously defined absolute value required"
  *  "Short branch out of range"
  *  "Illegal or missing opcode"
  *  "Illegal data in .bss segement"
  *  "EOF or END within .if"
  *  "Garbage character"
  *  "Word value too large"
  *  "Improper nesting of .if and .endif"
  *  "Missing label"
  *  "Multiply defined symbol"
  *  "Number syntax"
  *  "Cannot move location counter backwards"
  *  "Symbol value changed between passes"
  *  "Missing quote"
  *  "Relocation error"
  *  "Missing symbol"
  *  "Undefined symbol"
  *  "Illegal value (e.g. register >15)"
  *  "Syntax error"
  *  "Division by zero"
  *  "Too many numeric labels"

<br>
<b>10. Example</b>

The following assembler program prints out "Hello, world!" to the standard output on a Unix system.
<verbatim>
reset:	0xf000; start

start:	stwp	sp
	ai	sp,-6
	mov	@len,@4(sp)
	mov	@str,@2(sp)
	mov	@one,(sp)
	sys	4
	ai	sp,6
	idle

	.data
one:	1		// stdout
str:	1f		// &str
len:	strend - 1f	// len

1:	"Hello, world!\n"
	strend = .
</verbatim>

The assembler list output for the above program is:
<verbatim>
0000t                    00001  
0000t F000a 0004t        00002  reset:	0xf000; start
0004t                    00003  
0004t 02AFa              00004  start:	stwp	sp
0006t 022Fa FFFAa        00005  	ai	sp,-6
000At CBE0a 0028d 0004a  00006  	mov	@len,@4(sp)
0010t CBE0a 0026d 0002a  00007  	mov	@str,@2(sp)
0016t C7E0a 0024d        00008  	mov	@one,(sp)
001At 2C60a 0004a        00009  	sys	4
001Et 022Fa 0006a        00010  	ai	sp,6
0022t 0340a              00011  	idle
0024t                    00012  
0024t                    00013  	.data
0024d 0001a              00014  one:	1		// stdout
0026d 002Ad              00015  str:	1f		// &str
0028d 000Ea              00016  len:	strend - 1f	// len
002Ad                    00017  
002Ad 48656C6C6F2C2077a> 00018  1:	"Hello, world!\n"
0038d                    00019  	strend = .
0038d                    00020
</verbatim>

The suffix letter "t", "d" or "b" after the location denotes the segment that location is associated with.
The suffix letters for the assembled code denote the relocatability of that word:
  *  a = absolute, no relocation
  *  t = relocated with text segment
  *  d = relocated with data segment
  *  b = relacated with bss segment
  *  u = undefined
  *  U = undefined external
  
If the last word or byte value is followed by an angle bracket (">"), there are more words or bytes generated
for that particular line than shown.

The column preceding the source text in the listing is the (decimal) line number.
